solution:
A point's quadrant is decided by the SIGNS of its two co-ordinates; if either co-ordinate is 0 the point lies on an axis.

| Point | Co-ordinates | Quadrant / axis |
|---|---|---|
| A | \((-3, 2)\) | Quadrant II |
| B | \((-5, -2)\) | Quadrant III |
| K | \((3.5, 1.5)\) | Quadrant I |
| D | \((2, 10)\) | Quadrant I |
| E | \((37, 35)\) | Quadrant I |
| F | \((15, -18)\) | Quadrant IV |
| G | \((3, -7)\) | Quadrant IV |
| H | \((0, -5)\) | Y-axis |
| M | \((12, 0)\) | X-axis |
| N | \((0, 9)\) | Y-axis |
| P | \((0, 2.5)\) | Y-axis |
| Q | \((-7, -3)\) | Quadrant III |

Note H, N and P: an \(x\) co-ordinate of 0 means the point is at zero distance from the Y-axis, so it lies ON the Y-axis. M has \(y = 0\), so it lies on the X-axis.

Both co-ordinates positive means the point is to the right of the Y-axis and above the X-axis.
\(\therefore\) The point lies in **Quadrant I**.

Both co-ordinates negative means the point is to the left of the Y-axis and below the X-axis.
\(\therefore\) The point lies in **Quadrant III**.

\(x\) positive puts the point to the right of the Y-axis and \(y\) negative puts it below the X-axis.
\(\therefore\) The point lies in **Quadrant IV**.

\(x\) negative puts the point to the left of the Y-axis and \(y\) positive puts it above the X-axis.
\(\therefore\) The point lies in **Quadrant II**.

Draw two mutually perpendicular number lines meeting at the origin O, the horizontal one being the X-axis and the vertical one the Y-axis, and mark equal units on both.
To plot a point \((x, y)\), count \(x\) units along the X-axis (right if positive, left if negative) and then \(y\) units parallel to the Y-axis (up if positive, down if negative).

| Point | Co-ordinates | Where it falls |
|---|---|---|
| L | \((-2, 4)\) | 2 units left, 4 up - Quadrant II |
| M | \((5, 6)\) | 5 units right, 6 up - Quadrant I |
| N | \((-3, -4)\) | 3 units left, 4 down - Quadrant III |
| P | \((2, -3)\) | 2 units right, 3 down - Quadrant IV |
| Q | \((6, -5)\) | 6 units right, 5 down - Quadrant IV |
| S | \((7, 0)\) | 7 units right, on the X-axis |
| T | \((0, -5)\) | 5 units down, on the Y-axis |

(The book prints no answer for this question because the answer is the drawing itself.)

Plot A\((3,0)\) on the X-axis, B\((3,3)\) and C\((0,3)\) on the Y-axis, and join A to B and B to C.
Now seg OA lies along the X-axis and seg OC along the Y-axis, where O\((0,0)\) is the origin, so the closed figure formed is OABC.
Its four sides are OA \(= 3\), AB \(= 3\), BC \(= 3\) and CO \(= 3\), all equal, and \(\angle\)AOC \(= 90^\circ\) because the axes are perpendicular. Sides AB and OC are both parallel to the Y-axis and BC and OA are both parallel to the X-axis, so all four angles are right angles.
A quadrilateral with all sides equal and all angles right angles is a **square**.
\(\therefore\) The figure formed is a square of side 3 units.

A line parallel to the Y-axis has every point at the same distance from it, so its equation is of the form \(x = k\).
The line is 7 units from the Y-axis and to its LEFT, and points to the left of the Y-axis have a negative \(x\) co-ordinate.
\(\therefore k = -7\), and the equation of the line is \(x = -7\).

A line parallel to the X-axis has every point at the same distance from it, so its equation is of the form \(y = k\).
The line is 5 units from the X-axis and BELOW it, and points below the X-axis have a negative \(y\) co-ordinate.
\(\therefore k = -5\), and the equation of the line is \(y = -5\).

A line parallel to the Y-axis has an equation of the form \(x = k\), and every point on it has the same \(x\) co-ordinate.
The point Q\((-3, -2)\) lies on the line, and its \(x\) co-ordinate is \(-3\).
\(\therefore\) The equation of the line is \(x = -3\).
To draw it, mark \(-3\) on the X-axis and draw the line through that mark parallel to the Y-axis; it passes through Q\((-3,-2)\), and also through \((-3, 0)\), \((-3, 1)\), \((-3, 5)\) and so on.

[Textbook misprint: the question reads "X-axis and line x = -4 are parallel lines". The line x = -4 is parallel to the Y-AXIS and perpendicular to the X-axis, so as printed the question has no answer - the two lines meet. The printed key of 4 is the distance from the Y-axis, which is what the question means to ask, and the answer below is given on that reading. Read "X-axis" as "Y-axis".]

The line \(x = -4\) consists of all points whose \(x\) co-ordinate is \(-4\), so it is parallel to the **Y-axis**, 4 units to its left.
The distance between two parallel lines is the perpendicular distance between them, and here every point of the line \(x = -4\) is 4 units from the Y-axis.
\(\therefore\) The distance is **4 units**.

A graph is parallel to the X-axis when its equation fixes \(y\), and parallel to the Y-axis when its equation fixes \(x\).
\(x = 3\) fixes the \(x\) co-ordinate, so its graph is parallel to the **Y-axis**.

A graph is parallel to the X-axis when its equation fixes \(y\), and parallel to the Y-axis when its equation fixes \(x\).
\(y - 2 = 0\) means \(y = 2\), which fixes the \(y\) co-ordinate, so its graph is parallel to the **X-axis**.

A graph is parallel to the X-axis when its equation fixes \(y\), and parallel to the Y-axis when its equation fixes \(x\).
\(x + 6 = 0\) means \(x = -6\), which fixes the \(x\) co-ordinate, so its graph is parallel to the **Y-axis**.

A graph is parallel to the X-axis when its equation fixes \(y\), and parallel to the Y-axis when its equation fixes \(x\).
\(y = -5\) fixes the \(y\) co-ordinate, so its graph is parallel to the **X-axis**.

First check that the three points really are collinear, by comparing the slopes of two of the segments.
Slope of AB \(= \dfrac{-1 - 3}{6 - 2} = \dfrac{-4}{4} = -1\)
Slope of AC \(= \dfrac{5 - 3}{0 - 2} = \dfrac{2}{-2} = -1\)
The slopes are equal and the segments share the point A, so A, B and C are collinear.
The line through A\((2,3)\) with slope \(-1\) is \(y - 3 = -1(x - 2)\), that is \(x + y = 5\).
It meets the X-axis where \(y = 0\), giving \(x = 5\), that is at \((5, 0)\).
It meets the Y-axis where \(x = 0\), giving \(y = 5\), that is at \((0, 5)\).

Each equation fixes one co-ordinate, so each graph is a line parallel to an axis.
\(x + 4 = 0\) gives \(x = -4\) ..... parallel to the Y-axis
\(2x + 3 = 0\) gives \(x = -\dfrac{3}{2} = -1.5\) ..... parallel to the Y-axis
\(y - 1 = 0\) gives \(y = 1\) ..... parallel to the X-axis
\(3y - 15 = 0\) gives \(y = 5\) ..... parallel to the X-axis
Two lines parallel to the Y-axis and two parallel to the X-axis cross in \(2 \times 2 = 4\) points, and each point takes its \(x\) from one vertical line and its \(y\) from one horizontal line.
\(\therefore\) The points of intersection are \((-4, 1)\), \((-1.5, 1)\), \((-1.5, 5)\) and \((-4, 5)\).
(These four points are the corners of a rectangle of width \(2.5\) and height \(4\).)

Each of these is a linear equation in two variables, so its graph is a straight line and TWO points are enough to draw it (a third is a useful check).
For \(x + y = 2\) :

| \(x\) | 0 | 2 | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 2 | 0 | 1 |

Plot \((0,2)\), \((2,0)\) and \((1,1)\) and draw the line through them.

Each of these is a linear equation in two variables, so its graph is a straight line and TWO points are enough to draw it (a third is a useful check).
For \(3x - y = 0\), that is \(y = 3x\) :

| \(x\) | 0 | 1 | -1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 0 | 3 | -3 |

Plot \((0,0)\), \((1,3)\) and \((-1,-3)\) and draw the line through them. Note it passes through the origin, because \(x = 0\) gives \(y = 0\).

Each of these is a linear equation in two variables, so its graph is a straight line and TWO points are enough to draw it (a third is a useful check).
For \(2x + y = 1\), that is \(y = 1 - 2x\) :

| \(x\) | 0 | 1 | -1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 1 | -1 | 3 |

Plot \((0,1)\), \((1,-1)\) and \((-1,3)\) and draw the line through them.

Reading the figure, Q is 2 units to the left of the Y-axis and 2 units above the X-axis, and R is 4 units to the right and 1 unit below.
\(\therefore\) Q\((-2, 2)\) and R\((4, -1)\).

T lies ON the Y-axis, 1 unit below the origin, so its \(x\) co-ordinate is 0.
M lies ON the X-axis, 3 units to the right of the origin, so its \(y\) co-ordinate is 0.
\(\therefore\) T\((0, -1)\) and M\((3, 0)\).

The third quadrant is the region to the left of the Y-axis AND below the X-axis, that is where both co-ordinates are negative.
Of the points shown, only S lies there, at \((-3, -2)\).
\(\therefore\) **Point S** lies in the third quadrant.

A point has equal \(x\) and \(y\) co-ordinates when it lies on the line \(y = x\).
Checking the points shown - P\((1,3)\), Q\((-2,2)\), R\((4,-1)\), S\((-3,-2)\), T\((0,-1)\), M\((3,0)\) - none of them has its two co-ordinates equal.
The only such point in the figure is the origin **O**, whose co-ordinates are \((0, 0)\) and \(0 = 0\).

The quadrant is decided by the signs of the two co-ordinates; a zero co-ordinate puts the point on an axis.
\((5, -3)\) : \(x\) positive, \(y\) negative \(\Rightarrow\) **Quadrant IV**.

The quadrant is decided by the signs of the two co-ordinates; a zero co-ordinate puts the point on an axis.
\((-7, -12)\) : both negative \(\Rightarrow\) **Quadrant III**.

The quadrant is decided by the signs of the two co-ordinates; a zero co-ordinate puts the point on an axis.
\((-23, 4)\) : \(x\) negative, \(y\) positive \(\Rightarrow\) **Quadrant II**.

The quadrant is decided by the signs of the two co-ordinates; a zero co-ordinate puts the point on an axis.
\((-9, 5)\) : \(x\) negative, \(y\) positive \(\Rightarrow\) **Quadrant II**.

The quadrant is decided by the signs of the two co-ordinates; a zero co-ordinate puts the point on an axis.
\((0, -3)\) : the \(x\) co-ordinate is 0, so the point is at zero distance from the Y-axis \(\Rightarrow\) it lies on the **Y-axis**.

The quadrant is decided by the signs of the two co-ordinates; a zero co-ordinate puts the point on an axis.
\((-6, 0)\) : the \(y\) co-ordinate is 0, so the point is at zero distance from the X-axis \(\Rightarrow\) it lies on the **X-axis**.

Draw one pair of axes and plot all six points on it, counting \(x\) units horizontally from the origin and then \(y\) units vertically.

| Point | Co-ordinates | Where it falls |
|---|---|---|
| A | \((1, 3)\) | Quadrant I |
| B | \((-3, -1)\) | Quadrant III |
| C | \((1, -4)\) | Quadrant IV |
| D | \((-2, 3)\) | Quadrant II |
| E | \((0, -8)\) | on the Y-axis, 8 units below O |
| F | \((1, 0)\) | on the X-axis, 1 unit right of O |

Note that A, C and F all have \(x = 1\), so they lie on one line parallel to the Y-axis.
(The book prints no answer for this question because the answer is the drawing itself.)

Line LM is parallel to the Y-axis, and every point marked on it - L, P, R, Q, M - has \(x\) co-ordinate 3.
The distance of a line \(x = k\) from the Y-axis is \(|k|\).
\(\therefore\) The distance of line LM from the Y-axis is **3 units**.

All three points lie on line LM, so each has \(x\) co-ordinate 3; only the \(y\) co-ordinate has to be read off.
P is 2 units above the X-axis, Q is 1 unit below it, and R is ON the X-axis.
\(\therefore\) P\((3, 2)\), Q\((3, -1)\) and R\((3, 0)\).

L and M both lie on line LM, which is parallel to the Y-axis, so both have the same \(x\) co-ordinate, namely 3.
\(\therefore\) The difference between their \(x\) co-ordinates is \(3 - 3 = 0\).
(This is true of ANY two points on a line parallel to the Y-axis - that is exactly what makes the line vertical.)

A line parallel to the X-axis has an equation of the form \(y = k\), and its distance from the X-axis is \(|k|\).
So \(|k| = 5\) gives \(k = 5\) or \(k = -5\).
\(y = 5\) is the line 5 units ABOVE the X-axis and \(y = -5\) is the line 5 units BELOW it.
\(\therefore\) There are **two** such lines, \(y = 5\) and \(y = -5\).

The line \(x = a\) is parallel to the Y-axis, and every point on it is \(a\) units from the Y-axis measured along the X-direction.
A distance can never be negative, so if \(a\) is negative the line lies to the LEFT of the Y-axis and the distance is \(-a\).
Both cases are covered by the absolute value.
\(\therefore\) The distance between the Y-axis and the line \(x = a\) is \(|a|\).
(For example \(x = 4\) is 4 units from the Y-axis, and so is \(x = -4\).)
